lessons.title: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money

blocks.md:
Suppose your product sends every user prompt to the strongest model you can buy. Quality is high, and so is the bill. Chen, Zaharia and Zou (FrugalGPT, 2023) surveyed 12 commercial LLM APIs in March 2023 and found prices that differ by up to two orders of magnitude: processing 10 million input tokens cost USD 0.2 on GPT-J (via Textsynth) and USD 30 on GPT-4. GPT-J is a 6-billion-parameter open model from EleutherAI, served cheaply through the Textsynth API; GPT-4 was OpenAI's strongest model.

Their illustrative customer-service bot answers 360,000 queries a month with 1,800-token prompts and 80-token answers. At GPT-4's March 2023 prices (USD 0.03 per thousand input tokens, USD 0.06 per thousand output tokens) each query costs 1,800 tokens x USD 0.03 per thousand = USD 0.054 for its input plus 80 tokens x USD 0.06 per thousand = USD 0.0048 for its answer, about USD 0.0588. Times 360,000 queries that is USD 21,168, about USD 21.2K per month.

The waste is that many prompts do not need the strong model. "What is the capital of France?" gets the same answer from a small model. The RouteLLM paper (Ong et al., 2024) puts the gap at more than 50x for one model family (Claude 3 Haiku at USD 1.25 versus Claude 3 Opus at USD 75 per million output tokens) and estimates a **blended** price, mixing input and output tokens in the proportions of its training prompts (95 input, 264 output on average): about USD 24.7 per million tokens for GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106) and USD 0.24 for Mixtral 8x7B.

Mixtral 8x7B is an open model from Mistral AI built as a *mixture of experts*: each layer has 8 expert blocks, and a small gate picks 2 of them for every token, so each token uses about 13B of the model's 47B parameters. That is why it is cheap to serve.

The blended price is the average price per token of a typical request. GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106) charged USD 10 per million input tokens and USD 30 per million output tokens. A million average requests hold 95 million input and 264 million output tokens, so they cost 95 x 10 + 264 x 30 = USD 8,870 for 359 million tokens: 8,870 divided by 359 is about USD 24.7 per million tokens. The output tokens dominate because there are more of them and they cost three times as much. RouteLLM assumes one Mixtral price for input and output, so its blend is simply 0.24.

If a fraction $p$ of traffic goes to the strong model and the rest to the weak one, the blended cost is a weighted average:

blocks.caption: c_s and c_w are the strong and weak prices per million tokens. With a 100x price gap the strong term dominates: cost is roughly proportional to p, the share of strong calls.

scenes.caption: The two endpoints: GPT-4 at about 24.70 and Mixtral 8x7B at 0.24 USD per million tokens, a ratio of about 103x. These are the paper's 2024 estimates, used here only as a worked example.
Sending half the traffic to each model at random costs 0.5 x 24.70 + 0.5 x 0.24 = 12.47. Random mixing saves money but also loses quality on every hard prompt that lands on the weak model.
A router that sends only 30% of prompts to GPT-4 costs 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.58, about 3.3x cheaper than GPT-4 only. Whether quality survives depends on which 30% it picks.

blocks.md:
There are two ways to pick the model per prompt.

- **Routing** decides *before* generation. A small model called the **router** reads the prompt and sends it to exactly one LLM. One call per prompt.
- **Cascading** decides *after* generation. Call the cheap model first, judge its answer, and only if the answer looks unreliable call the next, more expensive model.

FrugalGPT groups cost-saving ideas into three families: prompt adaptation (shorter prompts), LLM approximation (caching answers, fine-tuning a cheaper model) and LLM cascades. This course covers cascades and routers; caching and prompt compression have their own course (semantic-caching-prompt-compression).

blocks.title: A router makes one decision before any LLM runs

scenes.caption: The router sits in front of both models. It sees only the prompt, never an answer, so its decision is a prediction about how much the strong model would help.
"What is the capital of France?": the router predicts the strong model would not do better, so the weak model answers. Cost for this prompt is about 1% of the strong model's.
"Find the race condition in this code": the router predicts a large quality gap, so the strong model answers. The user waits for one model only, plus the router's small overhead.

blocks.md: Routing pays off when two things are true at once: the price gap between models is large, and a sizable share of your prompts are ones where the weak model is just as good. If every prompt is hard, no router can save money without losing quality.

blocks.question: Using RouteLLM's blended prices (GPT-4 24.70, Mixtral 0.24 USD per million tokens), a router sends 30% of traffic to GPT-4. What is the blended cost per million tokens?
options: About 7.41, because only the GPT-4 share costs anything meaningful
About 12.47, the same as a 50/50 mix
About 7.58
About 17.36
blocks.explain: 0.3 x 24.70 + 0.7 x 0.24 = 7.41 + 0.168 = 7.58. Ignoring the weak model is a fine approximation here (7.41 is close) but not exact. 12.47 is the 50/50 mix and 17.36 corresponds to 70% strong.

blocks.question: Which statement correctly separates a router from a cascade?
options: A router calls every model and picks the best answer; a cascade calls one
A router chooses one model before generation; a cascade generates with a cheap model first and escalates only if the answer scores poorly
Both decide after generation, but a cascade uses a cheaper scorer
A router always costs more than a cascade because it runs a classifier
blocks.explain: Calling every model and picking the best answer is an ensemble (LLM-Blender does this), which costs the most. A router predicts from the prompt alone. A cascade sees an actual answer, which gives it more information but makes escalated prompts pay for several calls.

lessons.title: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure

blocks.md:
FrugalGPT's cascade has two parts. A **generation scoring function** $g(q, a)$ takes a query and an answer and returns a reliability score in $[0, 1]$. A **list** of $m$ APIs, ordered from cheap to expensive, has one threshold $\tau_i$ per tier. For each query the cascade calls tier 1, scores its answer, and returns it if the score is above $\tau_1$; otherwise it calls tier 2, and so on. The last tier's answer is always accepted.

The scorer is not an LLM. The paper trains a simple regression model that learns whether a generation is correct from the query and the answer; in its case study the scorer is a DistilBERT model, much smaller than any of the LLMs.

BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, Google, 2018) is a text encoder: it reads a whole text at once and turns it into vectors that a small output layer can map to a score. DistilBERT is BERT shrunk by *distillation*: a smaller student network is trained to reproduce BERT's outputs. Its authors report it is 40% smaller and 60% faster while keeping about 97% of BERT's language understanding, so scoring an answer costs almost nothing next to an LLM call.

blocks.caption: In words: z is the first tier whose answer scores above that tier's threshold, and the query's cost is the sum of the prices of tiers 1 through z. Every tier up to and including z is paid for, not just the one whose answer is returned.

blocks.md:
The list and the thresholds are learned together: maximize expected answer quality subject to an average cost budget. That is a mixed-integer problem: some choices are discrete (which models go in the list, and in what order) and others are continuous (the thresholds), so there is no smooth slope to follow and the number of possible lists grows combinatorially with the number of models. FrugalGPT uses a specialized optimizer that prunes lists whose models rarely disagree. The next lesson finds thresholds for a two-tier cascade by brute force, which is the same search without the pruning.

On HEADLINES (classifying gold-price news headlines as up, down, neutral or none) with a budget of USD 6.5, one fifth of GPT-4's cost on that dataset, the learned cascade was: GPT-J, accept if the score is above 0.96; otherwise J1-L (AI21's Jurassic-1 Large, a 7.5-billion-parameter model), accept if above 0.37; otherwise GPT-4. The paper reports 80% lower cost than GPT-4 with 1.5% higher accuracy. Across its datasets it reports matching the best single LLM with up to 98% cost reduction.

blocks.title: The cascade FrugalGPT learned on HEADLINES

scenes.caption: The learned strategy: three tiers and two thresholds. The thresholds are not equal; the optimizer set a very strict bar for GPT-J and a loose one for J1-L.
Query A: GPT-J's answer scores 0.98, above 0.96, so it is returned. Only the cheapest model and the tiny scorer ran. (Scores in these scenes are illustrative.)
Query B: GPT-J scores 0.41, so the cascade escalates. J1-L's answer scores 0.52, above 0.37, and is returned. This query paid for two LLM calls.
Query C: both cheap answers score low (0.12, then 0.20), so GPT-4 answers. This query paid for all three calls and waited for all three, which is the cascade's worst case.

blocks.title: Tracing query B through a cascade
blocks.code:
TIERS = [("gpt-j", 0.96), ("j1-large", 0.37), ("gpt-4", None)]

def cascade(query):
    spent = 0.0
    for model, tau in TIERS:
        answer = call(model, query)
        spent += price(model, query, answer)
        if tau is None:              # last tier: always accept
            return answer, model, spent
        score = scorer(query, answer)    # reliability in [0, 1]
        if score > tau:
            return answer, model, spent

scenes.caption: The tiers and thresholds come from the optimizer. The last tier has no threshold: whatever GPT-4 says is final.
Tier 1: GPT-J answers and we pay for it whether or not we keep the answer.
The scorer rates the answer 0.41. That is not above 0.96, so the loop moves on.
Tier 2: J1-L answers; its cost is added to what we already spent.
0.52 is above 0.37, so J1-L's answer is returned. GPT-4 never runs for this query.

blocks.md:
For a two-tier cascade where a fraction $e$ of queries escalate, expected cost per query is $c_w + e\,c_s$: the weak model runs on every query. A router that sends the same fraction $e$ to the strong model costs $e\,c_s + (1-e)\,c_w$.

Use RouteLLM's average request (95 input and 264 output tokens) and its prices: GPT-4 (USD 10 and USD 30 per million input and output tokens) costs about USD 8,870 per million queries, and Mixtral (USD 0.24 per million tokens) about USD 86. GPT-4's figure is lesson 1's 95 x 10 + 264 x 30 = 8,870; Mixtral's is 359 x 0.24 = 86, since its one price covers all 359 million tokens.

blocks.prompt: With e = 30% of queries escalating, how much more does the cascade cost than a router that sends the same 30% to GPT-4? And what does the cascade cost in latency?
blocks.reveal:
Cost: the cascade costs 86 + 0.3 x 8,870 = about USD 2,747 per million queries; the router costs 0.3 x 8,870 + 0.7 x 86 = about USD 2,721. Under 1% apart, because the cheap model is nearly free.

Latency is the real price. Assume the weak model takes 0.6 s, the scorer 0.02 s, the strong model 2.0 s and a router 0.03 s. Every escalated query in the cascade waits 0.6 + 0.02 + 2.0 = 2.62 s. Mean latency is 0.7 x 0.62 + 0.3 x 2.62 = 1.22 s for the cascade versus 0.03 + 0.7 x 0.6 + 0.3 x 2.0 = 1.05 s for the router.

blocks.title: Latency: cascade escalation versus a router (assumed timings)

scenes.caption: An easy query in a cascade: the weak model answers in 0.6 s and the scorer accepts it 0.02 s later. This is as fast as using the weak model alone.
A hard query in a cascade: the weak answer is generated and rejected first, then the strong model starts at 0.62 s. The user waits 2.62 s.

The same hard query through a router: 0.03 s to classify the prompt, then the strong model. Done at 2.03 s. It skips the wasted weak call but never sees an answer, so it can err where a scorer would not. Timings are assumed, not measured.

blocks.md:
Why use a cascade at all, then? Because judging an answer is easier than predicting from the prompt alone whether the cheap model will cope. A scorer can notice that an answer is malformed, hedged or inconsistent. AutoMix (Aggarwal et al.) takes this further: the small model checks its own answer with few-shot self-verification, and a router decides whether to escalate based on that noisy confidence. Few-shot means the verification prompt includes a few worked examples (AutoMix uses four) of a context, a question, an answer and a verdict. The small model is then asked whether its own answer is correct, the question is sampled several times with randomness turned up, and the fraction of "correct" verdicts is the confidence. The next lesson shows how AutoMix turns that noisy number into a decision.

Cascades fit best when answers are short (labels, extractions, yes or no), when latency is not critical (batch jobs), or when a cheap check of correctness exists, such as a schema validator or unit tests for generated code.

A scorer is only as good as the data it was trained on. Thresholds like 0.96 were tuned on one dataset's training split. A calibrated score matches how often answers are right (of answers scored 0.9, about 90 percent are correct); an overconfident one scores too high. On a new kind of query an overconfident scorer accepts wrong cheap answers silently: cost goes down and nobody notices that quality went down too. Track the acceptance rate per tier and audit a sample of accepted answers.

blocks.question: You raise the tier-1 threshold of a two-tier cascade from 0.96 to 0.99. What happens?
options: Fewer queries escalate, so cost falls
More queries escalate: cost and mean latency rise, and accuracy usually rises because fewer weak answers are accepted
Nothing changes, since the scorer's outputs are calibrated probabilities
The weak model is skipped for hard queries, so latency falls
blocks.explain: A stricter threshold accepts fewer cheap answers, so more queries pay for the strong model and wait for both calls. The weak model still runs on every query; a cascade cannot skip it, only a router can.

blocks.question: Which workload is the best fit for a cascade rather than a router?
options: A voice assistant with a 300 ms latency budget
A chat product where most answers are long essays
A nightly batch that labels support tickets into 12 categories, where a wrong label is cheap to detect
Any workload, because cascades are always more accurate
blocks.explain: Short answers make the wasted weak call cheap, a batch job does not care about the extra latency, and an easy correctness check makes the scorer reliable. A tight latency budget punishes escalation, and long answers make the wasted weak generation expensive.

lessons.title: Deferral signals: when should a cascade escalate?

blocks.md:
A cascade lives or dies by its **deferral rule**: given the cheap model's answer, keep it or escalate. Lesson 2's FrugalGPT trained a DistilBERT scorer for that, which needs labeled answers for every task. Before training anything, ask what signals you already have. There are four families:

1. The cheap model's own **token probabilities**.
2. **Consistency**: ask it several times and see whether the answers agree.
3. **Self-verification**: ask it whether its answer is right.
4. **External checkers**: a schema validator, a compiler, unit tests.

This lesson measures the first two on real outputs, then covers the other two and how to set thresholds.

A language model writes one token at a time and gives each a probability; its **log-probability** (natural log, so between minus infinity and 0) is what APIs usually return. In classification the standard deferral rule is **Chow's rule** (Chow, 1970): defer when the probability of the predicted label is low. Gupta et al. (Google Research, 2024) studied how to carry it to generated text, where an answer is a whole sequence of token probabilities and answers differ in length. They named three ways to turn the sequence into one score after Chow:

blocks.tex: s_{\text{sum}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p_i, \qquad s_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p_i, \qquad s_{\text{quant}}(\alpha) = \text{quantile}_{\alpha}(\log p_1, \ldots, \log p_n)
blocks.caption: p_i is the small model's probability for its own i-th output token; n is the answer length. Chow-Sum is the log of the whole answer's probability, Chow-Average divides by length, Chow-Quantile at alpha = 0 (a quantile level, not the later router alpha) is the least confident token. Escalate if low.

blocks.title: One answer, three ways to score it (toy probabilities)

scenes.caption: Ten output tokens of a toy answer. The model is sure of almost every token but hesitates on the result of the subtraction, the one token that matters.
Chow-Sum adds the logs: -1.07, a whole-answer probability of 0.34. Chow-Average divides by 10: -0.107, which looks confident because nine easy tokens dilute the shaky one.
Chow-Quantile at alpha = 0 takes the minimum, -0.89 at the token 9. A rule that escalates when any token is below probability 0.5 catches this answer; the average never would.

blocks.prompt: Answer A has 4 tokens, each with probability 0.9. Answer B has 40 tokens, each with probability 0.98. Under Chow-Sum, which answer looks less confident and is escalated first? Under Chow-Average?
blocks.reveal:
Chow-Sum: A scores 4 x ln 0.9 = -0.42 and B scores 40 x ln 0.98 = -0.81, so B is escalated first even though every one of its tokens is more confident than any of A's. Sums of negative numbers grow with length: that is the **length bias**.

Chow-Average: A scores -0.105 and B -0.020, so A goes first. Gupta et al. found exactly this pattern on FLAN-T5 cascades: Chow-Sum over-defers long outputs, and Chow-Average over-corrects and defers short ones.

blocks.md:
Their findings, on FLAN-T5 Base to Large cascades over classification, question answering and translation: Chow-Quantile beat both Sum and Average for a suitable quantile, but no single quantile was best on every dataset. The minimum (alpha = 0) caught repetitions and unknown tokens; a high quantile such as 0.8 focused on short uncertain outputs. Their best rule was learned: a 5-layer MLP over a vector of quantiles plus the Sum and Average scores, trained with logistic loss on labels saying "the large model is right and the small one wrong". Adding embeddings from the models helped further.

The practical lesson: if your API returns log-probabilities, try the minimum and a few quantiles, not only the average.

Now measure on real outputs. The weak model is Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, a 0.5-billion-parameter open model, run on a laptop CPU over the first 40 GSM8K test questions (grade-school math word problems with one numeric answer). For each question we keep its greedy answer (always the most likely next token) with the log-probability of every token, plus 3 answers sampled at temperature 0.7. The strong model is not run: we assume it answers every question correctly, so an escalated question always counts as right. Costs use lesson 2's per-query prices: USD 86 per million queries for a weak call, 8,870 for a strong one.

Alone, the weak model's greedy answers are right on 16 of 40 (0.400); the majority answer of its 3 samples is right on 19 (0.475).

blocks.caption: Run here on CPU with Hugging Face Transformers, 2 threads: about 28 s per question (19 minutes for 40); answers cut at 400 tokens. Qwen's generation config adds a 1.1 repetition penalty to every call, so greedy picks and log-probs are of the penalized distribution.
blocks.code:
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct").eval()
SYS = "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \\boxed{}."

for q, ref in questions:
    enc = tok([tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "system", "content": SYS},
                                        {"role": "user", "content": q}],
                                       tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)],
              return_tensors="pt")
    g = model.generate(**enc, do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=400,
                       output_scores=True, return_dict_in_generate=True)
    logp = model.compute_transition_scores(g.sequences, g.scores,
                                           normalize_logits=True)[0]   # log p per token
    s = model.generate(**enc, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=1.0, top_k=0,
                       num_return_sequences=3, max_new_tokens=400)
    # keep: final(greedy text), logp.tolist(), [final(t) for t in sampled texts]

logp = logp[:-1]                          # drop the end-of-text token
s_sum, s_avg, s_min = sum(logp), sum(logp) / len(logp), min(logp)
agree = votes.most_common(1)[0][1] / 3     # share of samples on the majority answer

blocks.title: The first 10 questions: signals and who gets escalated

scenes.caption: Real numbers for questions 1 to 10 (last token dropped, usually end-of-text). Wrong answers tend to be long: question 8 ran into the 400-token cap. Every answer has some token below probability 0.35, so the minimum is never close to 0.
Escalate the 3 lowest Chow-Sum scores: questions 3, 8 and 9, all wrong. Accuracy goes from 4 of 10 to 7 of 10. Here length bias helps, because length tracks errors on this model.
Escalate the 3 lowest minimum token log-probs: questions 6, 8 and 9, also all wrong: 7 of 10 again. The two signals disagree on which wrong answers they find.
Agreement below 2 of 3 escalates 7 of 10 questions. The majority answer is kept for 2, 4 and 7, and is right on 4 and 7: 9 of 10 correct, but at a 70% escalation rate.

blocks.title: Cascade accuracy versus escalation rate, 40 GSM8K questions

scenes.caption: The line is a cascade that escalates at random: escalating e% of questions fixes e% of the 60% that were wrong. Every signal beats it; Chow-Sum is best of the log-prob scores here (Chow-Average gives 0.700 at 40%).

Consistency (keep the majority of 3 samples if at least 2 agree) escalates 60% and reaches 0.925, against 0.875 for Chow-Sum at the same rate. 40 questions give a standard error near 5 points, so read the ranking loosely.

blocks.md:
What the run says, at this tiny scale. Wrong answers averaged 338 tokens against 258 for right ones, and all 6 answers that hit the 400-token cap were wrong; so the length bias of Chow-Sum points in a useful direction for this model, as Gupta et al. also saw when long outputs were repetitive. The minimum token probability is weaker here, because a long chain of reasoning always contains a few uncertain tokens. Consistency was the strongest signal (with one fixed sampling seed), and the cost of its two extra samples is small: 3 x 86 + 0.6 x 8,870 = USD 5,580 per million queries against 86 + 0.6 x 8,870 = 5,408 for Chow-Sum at the same 60% escalation, for 5 more points of accuracy.

On another model or task the ranking can flip, which is why you measure on your own outputs.

**Signal 2: consistency.** Yue et al. (ICLR 2024) observed that a weaker model's sampled answers tend to agree on easy questions and scatter on hard ones. Their **vote** rule samples $K$ answers, takes the most common one as the weak answer, and keeps it if the share of samples agreeing with it is at least a threshold $\tau$. Their **verify** rule asks in two different ways, for example a chain-of-thought prompt (reasoning in words) and a program-of-thought prompt (reasoning as Python code that is then run), and keeps the answer only if the two majority answers match.

With GPT-3.5-turbo as the weak model ($K$ = 20 samples) and GPT-4 as the strong one, the mixture of both prompt styles matched GPT-4's average accuracy over six reasoning datasets (0.929 against 0.931) at 40% of GPT-4's cost. Agreement across *different* prompts was a better signal than agreement across samples of one prompt.

**Signal 3: self-verification.** AutoMix (Aggarwal et al.) asks the small model, with a fixed 4-shot prompt, whether its answer is supported by the context, samples that verdict 8 times at temperature 1, and uses the share of "correct" verdicts as the confidence $v$. The simplest router escalates when $v$ is below a threshold.

The verdicts are noisy, so AutoMix adds a **meta-verifier**: a small decision model that treats $v$ as an *observation* of a hidden state rather than as the truth. The state says how well each model would do on this query; roughly, the query is easy (the small model is right), hard (only the large model is right) or unsolvable. From training data it learns how often each value of $v$ appears in each state, updates its belief after seeing $v$, and picks the action with the best expected reward, performance minus $\lambda$ times cost. Formally it is a POMDP (a decision process whose state is only partly observed); at inference it is a lookup that takes under a millisecond.

blocks.title: A one-step meta-verifier: belief after seeing the verdicts (toy)

scenes.caption: Before any verdicts, the training data says 55% of queries are easy, 20% hard and 25% unsolvable. Escalating gains only on hard queries and costs 0.25 in accuracy units (lambda times the strong model's price).
Low confidence (0 to 3 of 8 verdicts say correct): unsolvable queries produce this most often, so belief moves there: hard only 0.190. Escalating gains 0.190 for 0.25 in cost: keep the cheap answer.
Middle confidence (4 to 6 of 8): hard rises to 0.331, above the 0.25 cost, so escalate. A plain threshold on v cannot do this: it would escalate low scores even more eagerly than middle ones.
High confidence (7 or 8 of 8): easy 0.863, hard 0.105: keep the cheap answer. Simplified: AutoMix uses continuous states, kernel density estimates and a POMDP solver, not this 3-state table.

blocks.md:
The bars use Bayes' rule: belief in a state after seeing $v$ is proportional to its prior times how often that state produces $v$ (here easy gives low, middle, high with probability 0.1, 0.3, 0.6; hard 0.3, 0.5, 0.2; unsolvable 0.8, 0.15, 0.05). AutoMix reports that this kind of router, on its qasper results, learned to return the small model's answer for very low confidence instead of paying for a large model that would also fail.

**Signal 4: external checkers.** When the output has a machine-checkable form, check it: parse JSON against a schema, compile generated code, run unit tests, re-execute a computation. These checks are cheap and nearly deterministic, so a cascade built on them has a tiny judge error. The agent-verification course, which is not a prerequisite here, goes deeper into layering such checks and estimating their error rates.

**Choosing the threshold.** FrugalGPT's optimizer searches lists and thresholds together. For one cheap model and one strong model the search is small enough to do by brute force: on a labeled validation set, try every distinct score as the threshold, compute accuracy and cost, and keep the most accurate setting whose cost fits the budget. For three tiers you would loop over pairs of thresholds; FrugalGPT's pruning exists because with many models the number of possible lists explodes.

Below, the 40 questions are split alternately into 20 for validation and 20 for test, with a budget of USD 3,000 per million queries, which allows escalating at most (3,000 - 86) / 8,870 = 32.9% of queries.

blocks.title: Brute-force threshold sweep under a budget (real run)
blocks.code:
C_W, C_S, BUDGET = 86, 8870, 3000      # USD per million queries

def run(data, score, tau):
    esc = [r[score] < tau for r in data]
    e = sum(esc) / len(data)
    acc = sum(1 if z else r["ok"] for z, r in zip(esc, data)) / len(data)
    return e, acc, C_W + e * C_S

def sweep(data, score):
    best = None
    for tau in sorted({r[score] for r in data} | {float("-inf")}):
        e, acc, cost = run(data, score, tau)
        if cost <= BUDGET and (best is None or acc > best[1]):
            best = (tau, acc, e, cost)
    return best

tau, acc, e, cost = sweep(val, "sum")
print(run(test, "sum", tau))

scenes.caption: Each candidate threshold is one of the validation scores (plus minus infinity, which escalates nothing). Escalated questions count as right because the strong model is assumed correct.
Candidates that escalate more than 32.9% break the budget and are skipped; among the rest the most accurate wins.
Best on validation for Chow-Sum: tau = -41.83, escalating 30% at cost 2,747, accuracy 0.65 (from 0.35 without escalation on these 20 questions).
On the 20 test questions the same threshold escalates 50%: accuracy 0.90 but cost 4,521, far over the budget. Twenty questions cannot pin down a threshold.

blocks.md: A threshold is a quantile of the score distribution, so its cost depends on what traffic arrives. Tune it on hundreds or thousands of labeled queries that look like production, check it on a separate test split, and re-check it whenever the prompt, the weak model or the traffic changes. The same run with Chow-Average and the minimum token probability also moved from 25 to 30% escalation on validation to 50% on test.

A cascade decides once per answer. **Speculative cascades** (Narasimhan et al., Google Research, 2024) apply the deferral decision token by token: the small model drafts a few tokens, the large model scores them all in one parallel pass as in speculative decoding, and a deferral rule (such as Chow's rule on each token) decides which draft tokens to keep. Unlike speculative decoding, the output need not match the large model's distribution, so it can trade quality for speed; the paper reports better cost-quality trade-offs than either sequential cascades or speculative decoding on Gemma and T5 models. The draft-and-verify mechanics are covered in the speculative-decoding course, which is not a prerequisite here.

blocks.question: A consistency cascade samples the weak model k = 3 times, so the weak side costs 3 x 86 = 258 instead of 86 USD per million queries. The strong model costs 8,870. When is this still worth it?
options: Never, because tripling a cost can only make the cascade more expensive
When the agreement signal lets you escalate even a few percent fewer queries at the same accuracy, since each percent of escalation costs about 89 USD
Only if the three samples are run in parallel
Only when the weak model is more accurate than the strong one
blocks.explain: The extra 172 USD per million queries equals about 2% of escalation (0.02 x 8,870 = 177). If agreement ranks wrong answers better than log-probabilities, so that you escalate 2% fewer queries for the same accuracy, or catch more errors at the same rate, the extra samples pay for themselves. Running them in parallel helps latency, not cost.

blocks.question: Your cascade escalates on Chow-Sum, the log-probability of the whole answer. After a prompt change the weak model writes longer explanations, and the escalation rate jumps from 20% to 45% with no change in accuracy. What happened?
options: The weak model got worse
The strong model became cheaper
The scorer overfits to short prompts
Length bias: a sum of per-token log-probabilities falls as answers grow, so longer answers look less confident even when they are right
blocks.explain: Every extra token adds a negative term to the sum. Longer answers therefore score lower regardless of quality. Use a length-robust score (minimum token probability, a quantile, or a learned rule over several quantiles), and re-sweep the threshold whenever the prompt or output format changes.

blocks.question: In AutoMix's setting, why might a router decline to escalate a query whose self-verification confidence is very low?
options: Because the meta-verifier has learned that such queries are often unsolvable by any model, so paying for the large model would not improve the answer
Because low confidence always means the small model is right
Because escalation is disabled for low scores by default
Because the verifier's samples are too expensive to repeat
blocks.explain: The meta-verifier reasons about hidden states. If very low confidence mostly comes from queries no model can answer, escalating them spends money without gaining accuracy. Middle confidence, which more often comes from queries the large model can fix, is where escalation pays.

lessons.title: Learned routers: predict whether the strong model would win

blocks.md:
A router has to decide from the prompt alone. RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024, published at ICLR 2025, the International Conference on Learning Representations) frames this as binary routing between a **strong** model class (high quality, high cost; GPT-4 in their main experiments) and a **weak** one (Mixtral 8x7B), with one LLM call per query.

The router has two parts. A **win prediction model** estimates $P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q)$, the probability that the strong model's answer to prompt $q$ would be preferred over the weak model's. The subscript $\theta$ stands for the router's learned parameters. A **cost threshold** $\alpha \in [0,1]$ turns that probability into a decision.

blocks.tex: R^{\alpha}(q) = \begin{cases} M_{weak} & \text{if } P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q) < \alpha \\ M_{strong} & \text{if } P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q) \ge \alpha \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Route to the strong model when the predicted probability that it wins is at least alpha, and to the weak model otherwise. A higher alpha sends more traffic to the weak model (cheaper); a lower alpha favors the strong model. One trained router gives a whole family of operating points.

blocks.md:
The parameters $\theta$ are fit by maximum likelihood on **preference data**: triples of a prompt and a label saying whether the strong model won, the weak model won, or it was a tie.

*Maximum likelihood* means choosing $\theta$ so that the router gives the labels actually observed the highest possible probability: maximize the sum, over all training prompts, of $\log P_\theta(\text{label} \mid q)$. Logs turn the product of many probabilities into a sum; maximizing it is the same as minimizing the usual cross-entropy loss of a classifier.

The main source is about 80K battles from Chatbot Arena, where users compare two anonymous models and vote. Labels between any two specific models are sparse (on average, under 0.1% of the comparisons involve a given pair), so the authors cluster 64 models into 10 tiers by Arena score, take the top two tiers as strong and the third as weak, and keep only who won. After pruning prompts shorter than 16 characters, 65K comparisons remain.

The Arena score that ranks models comes from the **Bradley-Terry** model (1952). Give each model a strength $\xi$; model $i$ beats model $j$ with probability $\sigma(\xi_i - \xi_j) = 1 / (1 + e^{-(\xi_i - \xi_j)})$. Here $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid, which squashes any number into a probability between 0 and 1: equal strengths give 0.5, and a gap of 1 gives about 0.73. Fitting the strengths to all the votes by maximum likelihood ranks the models.

blocks.title: One router, four thresholds (toy prompts, illustrative scores)

scenes.caption: Ten toy prompts with the router's predicted win probability. At alpha = 0.8 only the race-condition bug goes to the strong model (S): 10% strong calls, blended cost 2.69 USD per million tokens.
alpha = 0.6 adds the proof and the tax calculation: 30% strong calls, cost 7.58.
alpha = 0.4 adds the SQL window query: 40% strong, cost 10.02. The router's ranking stays fixed; alpha only moves the cut.
alpha = 0.2 adds the regex, the summary and the idiom: 70% strong, cost 17.36. If the summary and idiom gain nothing from the strong model, those two calls are pure waste.

blocks.md:
RouteLLM tests its routers on three public benchmarks that recur through the rest of the course:

- **MMLU** (Massive Multitask Language Understanding): multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, from law to physics, scored as accuracy against an answer key.
- **MT Bench**: the 80 two-turn chat questions from the prerequisite course, graded 1 to 10 by a GPT-4 judge.
- **GSM8K** (Grade School Math 8K): about 8,500 grade-school math word problems, each with a single numeric answer.

Sparse human votes are not enough, especially for prompts unlike Arena's. RouteLLM augments the data two ways:

- **Golden labels**: about 1,500 MMLU validation questions. Each model's answer is compared to the answer key, which yields a win, loss or tie for free.
- **LLM-judge labels**: prompts from the Nectar dataset (a public set of chat prompts, each with seven model responses ranked by GPT-4) that already had GPT-4 responses, new Mixtral responses, and GPT-4 as a pairwise judge. About 120K samples for roughly USD 700 in total.

The judge part is the LLM-as-judge setup from the prerequisite course, used here to manufacture routing labels.

The paper compares four ways to parameterize $P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q)$. The first two embed prompts with OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small. An **embedding** model maps a text to a vector of numbers so that texts with similar meaning get nearby vectors, and the similarity of two prompts is the cosine of the angle between their vectors (1 for the same direction, near 0 for unrelated).

**Similarity-weighted ranking**: embed the new prompt, weight every training prompt by its similarity to it (weight $\gamma^{1 + S}$ with $\gamma = 10$), then fit Bradley-Terry strengths for strong and weak on the weighted battles. No training; the fit happens at inference time.

Here $S$ is that cosine similarity, rescaled by how close the training prompt's own nearest neighbor is, so the best matches sit near 1. With $\gamma = 10$, a training prompt with $S = 1$ gets weight $10^{2} = 100$ and an unrelated one with $S$ near 0 gets about $10^{1} = 10$: close battles count ten times as much, so the fitted strengths describe prompts like this one. The exponential form was the authors' choice because it worked best in practice.

**Matrix factorization**: learn a score $\delta(M, q)$ from a model embedding and a query embedding; $P = \sigma(\delta(M_s, q) - \delta(M_w, q))$.

$\delta(M, q)$ is a learned quality score for model $M$ on prompt $q$. Each model gets a learned vector, the prompt's embedding is projected to the same length, and $\delta$ combines the two like a weighted dot product. The name comes from recommender systems, which fill in a user-by-item rating matrix by factoring it into user vectors and item vectors; here the matrix is prompt by model. Passing the score difference through $\sigma$ is the Bradley-Terry rule again, with $\delta$ as a per-prompt strength.

blocks.tex: \delta(M, q) = w_2^{\top}\big(v_m \odot (W_1^{\top} v_q + b)\big), \qquad P_\theta(\text{win}_s \mid q) = \sigma\big(\delta(M_s, q) - \delta(M_w, q)\big)
blocks.caption: v_q is the prompt's embedding and v_m the model's learned vector. W_1 and b project the prompt to the model vector's length; the circled dot multiplies the two vectors element by element; w_2 sums the result with learned weights into one score.

blocks.md:
A toy with 3 numbers per vector. Say the projection turns the prompt into $u = W_1^{\top} v_q + b = (0.5, -1, 2)$, the strong model's vector is $(0.8, 0.1, 0.6)$, the weak model's $(0.6, 0.3, 0.1)$ and $w_2 = (1, 1, 1)$. Element by element, the strong model gets $0.4 - 0.1 + 1.2 = 1.5$ and the weak one $0.3 - 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.2$. Then $P = \sigma(1.5 - 0.2) = \sigma(1.3) = 0.786$: routed to the strong model at alpha 0.5, to the weak one at alpha 0.8.

The third coordinate did most of the work: this prompt loads on a direction where the strong model's vector is large. In the released code the vectors have 128 numbers, the model vectors are scaled to length 1, and the projection and output layers have no bias term.

**Ties.** Preference labels are win, loss or tie, but each router uses ties differently. The released matrix factorization training script keeps only battles with a winner and maximizes $\log \sigma(\delta(\text{winner}, q) - \delta(\text{loser}, q))$, so ties are dropped. The BERT router instead predicts three classes, and its $P(\text{win}_s)$ is one minus the probabilities of tie and weak win: a likely tie pushes the prompt toward the cheap model, which is what you want when both answers are equally good.

**BERT classifier**: fine-tune BERT-base with a logistic head on its classification token. BERT-base is the 110-million-parameter version of the encoder from lesson 2. BERT puts a special classification token at the start of the input, and that token's output vector summarizes the whole prompt; a logistic head is one linear layer plus a sigmoid that turns the vector into $P_\theta$.

**Causal LLM classifier**: fine-tune Llama 3 8B to emit the label as a next token. *Causal* means an ordinary left-to-right text generator, where each token sees only the tokens before it; Llama 3 8B is Meta's open 8-billion-parameter model.

Step back and you can see three families of **router signals**, whoever builds the router:

- **Prompt classifiers** (BERT, causal LLM, matrix factorization): read the prompt, predict difficulty or the win probability. Cheap and pre-generation.
- **Similarity to past prompts**: look up prompts you have already seen with known outcomes, as in similarity-weighted ranking or a k-nearest-neighbor vote. Needs an embedding call and an index.
- **Judge or confidence on an answer**: score a cheap model's actual output, as in FrugalGPT's scorer or AutoMix's self-verification. More information, but only available after a generation, which makes it a cascade.

Treat alpha as a cost knob, not a quality guarantee. The predicted probabilities are rarely well calibrated (the calibration idea from lesson 2, applied here: among prompts given 0.7, the strong model should really win about 70% of the time), so choose alpha on a held-out set from your own traffic: pick the value that gives the share of strong calls (and hence the cost) you can afford, then measure quality at that point.

blocks.question: RouteLLM's routers trained only on Chatbot Arena data performed close to a random router on MMLU and GSM8K, while most of them beat random on MT Bench. What is the most likely explanation?
options: MMLU and GSM8K are too easy for the strong model
The test prompts are unlike the training prompts, so the win predictor has not learned their difficulty
The routers were not given enough GPU memory at inference
Random routing is optimal for multiple-choice questions
blocks.explain: The paper attributes it to most MMLU questions being out of distribution for Arena data. Adding about 1,500 golden-labeled MMLU validation questions, under 2% of the training data, made every router beat random on MMLU.

blocks.question: Which RouteLLM router does its fitting at inference time instead of during training?
options: The causal LLM classifier
Matrix factorization
The BERT classifier
Similarity-weighted ranking
blocks.explain: Similarity-weighted ranking solves a weighted Bradley-Terry problem for each new prompt, weighting training battles by similarity. That is why it needs no training, and also why it was the slowest router to serve.

lessons.title: Evaluating routers: cost-quality curves, PGR, APGR and CPT

blocks.md:
A router has two numbers that pull against each other. RouteLLM measures **cost** as $c$, the percentage of calls sent to the strong model, and **quality** as $r$, the average response score on a benchmark (accuracy on MMLU, a 1 to 10 judge rating on MT Bench).

Because a router's quality always lies between the weak model's and the strong model's, the paper normalizes it as the **performance gap recovered**, PGR for short: the share of the quality gap between the weak and the strong model that the router closes.

blocks.caption: PGR is the router's score minus the weak model's, over the strong model's score minus the weak model's: 1 means the router matches the strong model, 0 the weak one. APGR, the average performance gap recovered, averages PGR at ten cost levels: the area under the PGR versus strong-call-share curve.

blocks.md:
Neither number works alone: a router that always picks the strong model has PGR = 1 and saves nothing. So the paper sweeps $\alpha$, plots PGR against the share of strong calls, and reports two summaries:

- **APGR**, the area under that curve. A router that routes at random gets about 0.5, because on average a random $c\%$ of strong calls recovers $c\%$ of the gap.
- **CPT(x%)**, the call-performance threshold: the minimum share of strong calls needed to reach a PGR of x%. Lower is better.

blocks.title: PGR versus share of strong calls (simplified curve family)

x.label: % of calls to the strong model

scenes.caption: Stand-in curves: PGR = 1 minus (1 minus c) to the power k, with c the share of strong calls; a larger k is a sharper router. k = 1 is the diagonal, a random router: CPT(50%) = 50%, APGR = 0.5. Simplified, not a fit to real data.
k = 2.5: the router sends the prompts that gain most from the strong model first, so PGR rises quickly. CPT(50%) falls to 24.2% and APGR is 0.714.
k = 5: CPT(50%) is 12.9% and APGR 0.833, close to what RouteLLM's best MT Bench router reports (CPT(50%) of 13.40%, APGR 0.802).

blocks.md: Where those numbers come from: CPT(50%) is the share $c$ where the curve reaches 0.5. Setting $1 - (1 - c)^k = 0.5$ gives $(1 - c)^k = 0.5$, so $c = 1 - 0.5^{1/k}$, one minus the k-th root of one half. For $k = 2.5$ that is 1 minus 0.758, or 0.242, and for $k = 5$ it is 1 minus 0.871, or 0.129. APGR is the area under the curve: the area under $(1 - c)^k$ from 0 to 1 is $1/(k + 1)$, so APGR is $1 - 1/(k + 1)$, which is 2.5 divided by 3.5, or 0.714, and 5 divided by 6, or 0.833.

Now do it by hand on the ten toy prompts from the last lesson. Each prompt has a quality score for the weak and for the strong model (1 to 10, invented for this example). Averages: weak 6.5, strong 8.4, a gap of 1.9 points. Sweeping $\alpha$:

- $\alpha$ = 0.8: 10% strong, average 7.0, PGR 0.263, blended cost 2.69
- $\alpha$ = 0.6: 30% strong, average 7.6, PGR 0.579, cost 7.58
- $\alpha$ = 0.4: 40% strong, average 8.0, PGR 0.789, cost 10.02
- $\alpha$ = 0.2: 70% strong, average 8.3, PGR 0.947, cost 17.36

Each PGR is the average minus 6.5, divided by the 1.9 gap; for example 7.0 minus 6.5 is 0.5, and 0.5 divided by 1.9 is 0.263. Each cost is lesson 1's weighted average: at 10% strong, 0.1 x 24.70 + 0.9 x 0.24 = 2.69. Costs are USD per million tokens with RouteLLM's blended prices (24.70 strong, 0.24 weak). At $\alpha$ = 0.4 you keep 79% of the quality gap for 41% of the GPT-4-only price.

blocks.title: Toy router: blended USD per 1M tokens at each threshold

scenes.caption: Cost falls almost linearly with the share of strong calls, because the weak model is about 100x cheaper. All strong: 24.70; all weak: 0.24.
Same thresholds, now showing PGR x 100 (share of the quality gap kept). Quality falls slowly at first and then fast: the last prompts moved to the weak model are the ones that needed the strong one.

blocks.prompt: Your quality target is PGR of at least 80% on the toy set. Which alpha do you choose, and what does it cost?
blocks.reveal: alpha = 0.4 gives PGR 0.789, just short of 0.80, so you must go down to alpha = 0.2: PGR 0.947 at 70% strong calls and 17.36 USD per million tokens. On a ten-prompt set the CPT curve moves in big steps; on real traffic you would search alpha finely on a large held-out set. Notice how much the last 1% of target costs: from 10.02 to 17.36.

blocks.md:
What did RouteLLM measure? On MT Bench routing between GPT-4 and Mixtral 8x7B, a random router has CPT(50%) of 49.03%, CPT(80%) of 78.08% and APGR 0.500. The matrix factorization router trained on Arena plus judge-labeled data reaches CPT(50%) of 13.40%, CPT(80%) of 31.31% and APGR 0.802. The BERT router trained on Arena data alone scored APGR 0.391, worse than random, which the authors attribute to a large model in a low-data regime.

The paper converts this into cost savings: the random router's share of GPT-4 calls divided by the best router's share at the same PGR. On MT Bench at CPT(50%) that is 49.03% divided by 13.40%, or 3.66x. There, PGR 50% means 95% of GPT-4's quality: GPT-4 scores 9.3 on MT Bench, the router at CPT(50%) scores 8.8, and 8.8 divided by 9.3 is about 0.95. The same calculation gives only 1.41x on MMLU and 1.49x on GSM8K. The same routers, without retraining, also beat random when the pair was swapped to Claude 3 Opus and Sonnet or to Llama 3.1 70B and 8B (best APGR 0.772 and 0.767).

Read router claims carefully. "2x cheaper at the same quality" depends on the benchmark, the model pair, the quality target and the baseline. RouteLLM's savings are measured against a random router, not against a GPT-4-only deployment, and vary from 1.41x to 3.66x across three benchmarks. Only an evaluation on your own prompts tells you what you will get.

blocks.question: A router has r = 7.6 on a benchmark where the weak model scores 6.5 and the strong model 8.4. What is its PGR?
blocks.explain: PGR = (7.6 - 6.5) / (8.4 - 6.5) = 1.1 / 1.9 = 0.579. 0.905 is 7.6 / 8.4, which ignores the weak baseline; 0.421 is 1 minus the right answer.

blocks.question: Router A has APGR 0.80. Router B has APGR 0.75 but needs fewer strong calls than A to reach PGR 95%. Your product must stay at 95% of the strong model's quality gap. Which router should you prefer?
options: A, because APGR summarizes everything
Neither, because APGR below 0.9 is unusable
B, because what matters is the cost at your operating point, here CPT(95%)
A, because a higher area always means lower cost at every point
blocks.explain: APGR averages over all cost levels, most of which you will never run at. Curves can cross, so the router that is better on average can be worse at the one operating point you care about. RouteLLM reports CPT at specific targets for this reason.

lessons.title: Routing among many models: the cost-quality frontier

blocks.md:
So far every router chose between two models. Real deployments often have four or five: a tiny model, a mid-size open model, a fast commercial model and a frontier model. PGR from the evaluation lesson does not stretch to this case, because it measures the share of the gap between exactly one weak and one strong model.

Take a toy fleet: **tiny**, **small**, **mid** and **large**, costing 0.1, 0.5, 2 and 10 USD per 1,000 queries, and 12 prompts on which each model is either right or wrong. Alone, they score 5, 7, 7 and 11 of the 12 (accuracy 0.417, 0.583, 0.583 and 0.917). One prompt defeats every model. All numbers here are invented for the example and computed by a short script.

The binary rule generalizes directly. Predict, for each model $m$, how good its answer to prompt $q$ would be, $\hat{P}_m(q)$, then pick the model with the best predicted quality after paying for it. RouterBench (Hu et al., 2024, from Martian) writes the score as $\lambda \cdot P_{ij} - \text{cost}_j$ and calls $\lambda$ the **willingness to pay**: how much cost one unit of quality is worth to you. A higher $\lambda$ buys quality at a higher price; sweeping it traces the router's cost-quality curve, just as sweeping alpha did for RouteLLM.

The predictor can be anything that outputs a number per model: RouterBench trains a kNN and an MLP per task, and RouteLLM's matrix factorization already gives a score $\delta(M, q)$ for each of the 64 Arena models in its released code.

blocks.caption: Route prompt q to the model with the highest predicted quality times lambda, minus its price. With two models and a predicted win probability this reduces to a threshold, like RouteLLM's alpha.

blocks.title: Predicted quality per prompt and model, and the lambda router's pick

scenes.caption: A predictor's estimate that each model answers each prompt correctly (toy values). Easy prompts are high across the row; hard prompts are high only for large.
lambda = 3: one unit of accuracy is worth 3 USD per 1,000 queries, so large (10) never pays off. The router picks tiny on 5 prompts and small on 7: cost 0.333, accuracy 0.667.
lambda = 12: mid now wins prompts 7, 9 and 11, where its predicted quality beats small's by enough to cover the extra 1.5. Cost 0.875, accuracy 0.750.
lambda = 40: large takes 5 prompts and mid 4. Cost 4.958, accuracy 0.917: the same accuracy as large alone at half its price.

blocks.md:
To judge such a router, first ask what you could get with no router at all. RouterBench's answer starts with **linear interpolation**: send each query to model A with probability $t$ and to B otherwise, and by linearity of expectation the cost and quality land on the straight line between A and B. Any point inside the **convex hull** of the single-model points, the smallest convex shape that contains them all, can be reached this way.

Only the upper edge matters, and only while it rises: if paying more does not buy quality, you would just spend less. That rising upper edge is the **non-decreasing convex hull**. RouterBench calls the router that mixes models at random along it the **Zero router**: a learned router is worth its complexity only if its curve lies above this one.

blocks.title: Four models, their hull, the oracle and a lambda router

scenes.caption: Each model is one point; the x axis is logarithmic. The hull joins tiny, small and large. Mid sits below it: at cost 2 a random small/large mix already reaches 0.636, more than mid's 0.583.

The oracle sends each prompt to the cheapest model that answers it correctly: accuracy 0.917 for 2.008, large's quality at a fifth of its price. It needs knowledge of the answers, so it is an upper bound, not a router.

The lambda router at 3, 12 and 40 sits well above the hull (0.667 against 0.514 at cost 0.333). On real benchmarks the gap is far smaller, because real predictors are much noisier than these toy ones.

blocks.prompt: Mid is below the hull: as a single model it is never the best buy. Should you remove it from the router's pool?
blocks.reveal: Not necessarily. Mid alone is dominated, but on prompts 7, 9 and 11 the predictor expects it to beat small at a fraction of large's price, and the lambda = 12 router uses it exactly there. Being below the hull says a model is never worth using *for all traffic*; a per-prompt router can still find the slice where it is the best buy. RouterBench saw the same effect: its oracle often picks cheap models with about 50% average accuracy, because on many prompts they are right.

blocks.md:
**RouterBench** (arXiv 2403.12031) made this the standard comparison. It holds 405,467 pre-generated inference outcomes from 11 models on 8 datasets and 64 tasks (MMLU, MT-Bench, MBPP, GSM8K, HellaSwag, Winogrande, ARC-Challenge, plus a RAG set of 800 real user queries), so a router can be evaluated without calling any model.

The oracle shows how much room there is. On MMLU, GPT-4 alone scores 0.828 at a total cost of 4.086 USD on the benchmark, while the oracle reaches 0.957 for 0.297. GPT-4 is seldom the oracle's choice, and WizardLM-13B and Mistral-7B, at about 50% accuracy, are picked often because they are cheap and right on many prompts.

The learned routers did not come close to that oracle. RouterBench's kNN and MLP routers, trained on 70% of each task and tested on the rest, matched the best single model at lower or similar cost, but did not significantly beat the Zero router: higher **AIQ** on MMLU and Winogrande, comparable on HellaSwag and GSM8K, lower on ARC-Challenge and MBPP. AIQ, the average improvement in quality, is the area under a router's non-decreasing convex hull divided by the cost range: the many-model cousin of APGR.

RouterBench also simulated cascades whose judge is wrong with probability $\epsilon$. With $\epsilon$ up to 0.1 they beat every single model and the Zero router by a wide margin; above 0.2 their performance fell off quickly. A cascade is only as good as its deferral signal.

blocks.caption: R tilde is the non-decreasing convex hull of the router's points (one per lambda). Higher is better; compare it with the Zero router's AIQ over the same cost range.

blocks.md:
**Domain or specialist routing** (send code to a code model, legal questions to a fine-tuned model) is the same rule with a different predictor: $\hat{P}_m(q)$ comes from a topic classifier or from per-domain accuracy measured on your data. RouterBench's RAG set shows a case where the right specialist depends on the question: for news after GPT-4's knowledge cutoff, routers are expected to pick models with live web search.

Chat products now route between response modes too: OpenAI describes GPT-5 as a fast model, a deeper reasoning model and "a real-time router that quickly decides which to use based on conversation type, complexity, tool needs, and your explicit intent", retrained on signals such as users switching models and measured correctness.

Whatever the predictor, plot the result as points on the cost-quality plane and compare against the hull of the models you already have.

**Hybrid LLM** (Ding et al., Microsoft, ICLR 2024) is the binary relative of this lesson, worth knowing for how it builds labels. Its router, a DeBERTa-v3-large encoder (300M parameters), predicts the probability that the small model's answer is at least as good as the large model's, scored with BARTScore (an automatic text-quality metric). Because answers vary between samples, the soft label averages 10 sampled responses per model. When the large model is much stronger that probability is near 0 for most prompts, so labels are relaxed to "small is within $t$ of large", with $t$ chosen by grid search to spread the labels apart.

Reported result: 22% fewer calls to GPT-3.5-turbo (sent to Llama-2 13B instead) with about a 1% drop in BARTScore, and up to 40% fewer large-model calls with no drop for closer model pairs.

Compare a multi-model router against the non-decreasing convex hull of the models it routes between, not against the strongest model. Beating GPT-4's price at GPT-4's quality is easy if a random mix of cheaper models already does it.

blocks.question: A new model costs 3 USD per 1,000 queries and scores 0.60 on your traffic. Your current models give a hull value of 0.67 at that cost. Which statement is right?
options: Add it as the default model, because it is cheaper than the frontier model
It can never help, so ignore it completely
It is never worth sending all traffic to, but a per-prompt router may still use it on the prompts where it beats the cheaper models
It raises the hull because it adds a new point
blocks.explain: A random mix of existing models already gets 0.67 at 3 USD, so the model alone is dominated and the hull does not move. A per-prompt router can still use it on a slice of prompts where its predicted quality per dollar is best, as the toy router used mid.

blocks.question: With lambda = 12 and toy prices tiny 0.1, small 0.5, mid 2, large 10, a prompt has predicted quality tiny 0.1, small 0.3, mid 0.6, large 0.85. Which model does the router choose?
options: tiny
large
small
mid
blocks.explain: Scores are 12 x quality minus cost: tiny 1.1, small 3.1, mid 5.2, large 0.2. Mid wins: large adds 0.25 predicted quality, worth 3 at lambda 12, for 8 more in cost.

lessons.title: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail

blocks.md:
You do not have to train a router yourself. Amazon Bedrock is AWS's managed service that serves *foundation models* (large models pretrained on broad data and used for many tasks, such as Anthropic's Claude, Meta's Llama and Amazon's own Nova) from several providers behind one API. Bedrock **Intelligent Prompt Routing** is documented as "a single serverless endpoint to efficiently route requests between different foundational models within the same model family". Serverless means you call the endpoint and pay per request, with no servers of your own to run. For each request it predicts the response quality of each model from the prompt and routes to the one with the best combination of quality and cost. The response says which model handled it.

There are **default prompt routers**, preconfigured by AWS, and **configured prompt routers**. When you configure one, the docs say you must choose exactly two models within the same family, a **fallback model**, and a **routing criterion**: the response quality difference.

The fallback model is the anchor. In the docs' example, with a response quality difference of 10% and Amazon Nova Lite (the cheaper of the two) as the fallback, the router switches to the other model (say Nova Pro, a stronger and pricier model in Amazon's Nova family) only if its predicted response quality is more than 10% better than Nova Lite's.

The documented limitations matter as much as the features: routing is optimized only for English prompts, it cannot adjust decisions using application-specific performance data, and it may not route optimally for unique or specialized use cases because its effectiveness depends on its initial training data. AWS's product page claims routing "can reduce costs by up to 30% without compromising on accuracy"; that is AWS's own claim, not a measured result you can assume for your traffic. The supported model list varies by Region (each of AWS's geographic data-center locations) and changes over time, so check the docs.

blocks.caption: Creating a configured router with the AWS CLI, the aws command-line tool (placeholders in angle brackets). The API takes the criterion on a 0 to 100 scale, so 10 most likely stands for the docs' 10%. CreatePromptRouter takes fallbackModel as one object; the user guide's example wraps it in a list.

blocks.md: Why 10 and not 0.1: the [API reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_RoutingCriteria.html) types `responseQualityDifference` as a number from 0 to 100, which suggests the value is in percentage points, so the docs' example of a 10% difference would be written as 10. The user guide's own CLI example passes 0.5, which on that scale would mean half a percent, and a third-party [Classmethod blog post](https://dev.classmethod.jp/articles/amazon-bedrock-supports-custom-prompt-routing/) reports the API rejecting values that are not multiples of 5 (the documentation does not mention that rule). Check the current console or API behavior before relying on a specific value.

blocks.title: A configured router with Nova Lite as fallback (10% criterion)

scenes.caption: Prompt 1 is a simple rewording task. The router predicts Nova Pro would be only 4% better (illustrative; AWS does not document the predictor's internals).
4% is below the 10% criterion, so the request goes to the fallback model. The response carries the id of the model that answered, which you should log.
Prompt 2 is a multi-step proof. The router predicts Nova Pro would be 25% better.
25% clears the criterion, so Nova Pro answers. One model call per request, as in RouteLLM; the router's own work happens before the call.

blocks.md:
**Failure mode 1: router drift.** A router learns the difficulty of the prompts it was trained on. RouteLLM's Arena-trained routers were near or below random on MMLU and GSM8K, and the paper found router quality tracked a benchmark-dataset similarity score: for each benchmark prompt, take the cosine similarity between its embedding and the closest training prompt's embedding, then average over the benchmark. The less a benchmark looked like the training data, the worse the routers did on it. In production the drift comes from you: a new feature, a new language, a new customer segment, or swapping in newer models. Bedrock's English-only optimization is the same issue stated up front.

Watch the share of strong calls over time (a sudden change means the input distribution moved) and keep auditing a sample of weak-model answers against the strong model.

**Failure mode 2: judge bias in the labels.** When routing labels come from an LLM judge, the router learns what the judge prefers. Zheng et al. (2023), who introduced MT Bench and studied GPT-4 as a judge, document position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. A router trained on such labels can learn "send it to the model that writes longer answers" rather than "send it to the model that is right". RouteLLM followed that paper's debiasing practices; mix in labels you trust (golden answers, human votes) and evaluate on them.

**Failure mode 3: the router's own cost and latency.** RouteLLM measured serving costs: matrix factorization handled 155.16 requests per second on one NVIDIA L4 GPU (USD 3.32 per million requests), while similarity-weighted ranking managed 2.9 per second on a CPU-only n2-standard-8 VM, a Google Cloud machine with 8 virtual CPUs (USD 39.26 per million). Even the most expensive added at most 0.4% to GPT-4 generation cost. Latency is different: the embedding call and classifier sit before the first token of every request.

Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

blocks.question: A Bedrock router uses Nova Lite as fallback with a 10% response quality difference. For a prompt, Nova Pro's predicted quality is 6% better than Nova Lite's. Which model answers?
options: Nova Pro, because it is predicted to be better
Both, and the router returns the better answer
Nova Lite, because 6% does not exceed the 10% criterion
Neither: the request fails and must be retried
blocks.explain: The criterion sets how much better the other model must be predicted to be before the router leaves the fallback. 6% is below 10%, so Nova Lite answers. Bedrock calls one model per request; it does not generate both and compare.

blocks.question: After launching in Japan, your router's share of strong-model calls drops from 35% to 12% and complaints about answer quality rise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The strong model became cheaper
Input distribution shift: the router misjudges the difficulty of prompts unlike its training data and sends hard ones to the weak model
Judge bias toward longer answers
The router's GPU is overloaded
blocks.explain: A sudden change in routing mix plus worse quality right after new traffic arrives points to drift. Bedrock's docs say its routing is optimized only for English prompts, and RouteLLM's routers fell to near random on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

blocks.question: Your router's training labels come from an LLM judge, and you notice it sends almost every prompt that asks for a list to the strong model. Which fix targets the likely cause?
options: Add trusted labels (golden answers or human votes) and evaluate the router on them, controlling for answer length
Lower alpha so more prompts reach the strong model
Replace the router with a cascade
Use a larger embedding model
blocks.explain: If the judge prefers longer, more detailed answers (verbosity bias), the router learns to route on length-related features. Trusted labels and an evaluation that controls for length expose and correct that. Moving alpha only shifts the cut; it does not fix what the router learned.

lessons.title: Build and run a router in production

blocks.md:
Every router so far came from a paper. This lesson builds one in about 30 lines, compares it with RouteLLM as a drop-in library, and then covers what happens around a router in production: fallbacks when a provider fails, conversations that span many turns, and how to keep measuring.

**The data.** The public Chatbot Arena dataset holds 57,477 human votes between two anonymous models. Following RouteLLM's tiers, keep single-turn battles of at least 16 characters between a top-two-tier model (GPT-4 versions, Mistral Medium, Claude 1, Qwen1.5-72B) and a third-tier model (Mixtral 8x7B, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B and others): 9,860 prompts. The stronger model won 46% of them, the weaker one 23%, and 30% were ties.

The label to predict is "the strong model won", so a tie counts as not winning, as in RouteLLM's BERT router. Quality needs a number per routed answer: score 1 if the routed model's answer was not beaten (it won or tied), else 0. On the test split that gives 0.766 for always-strong and 0.540 for always-weak, the two ends of the PGR scale.

Prompts are embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a small open sentence-embedding model (384 numbers per prompt; 23 seconds for all 9,860 on CPU; text past 256 word pieces is cut off, so long prompts are judged by their start). The split is 60% train, 20% calibration (for choosing alpha) and 20% test.

blocks.caption: The router core, run here on CPU (embedding, training and evaluation take under 30 seconds in total). y = 1 if the strong model won; ok_s and ok_w = 1 if that model's answer was not beaten.
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

enc = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
X = enc.encode(prompts, normalize_embeddings=True)          # (9860, 384)
# rows were shuffled once (numpy default_rng(0).permutation) before this
tr, ca, te = slice(0, 5916), slice(5916, 7888), slice(7888, 9860)

lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(X[tr], y[tr])
def p_logreg(Q): return lr.predict_proba(Q)[:, 1]
def p_knn(Q, k=50):                       # share of strong wins among k neighbors
    top = np.argpartition(-(Q @ X[tr].T), k, axis=1)[:, :k]
    return y[tr][top].mean(axis=1)

r_s, r_w = ok_s[te].mean(), ok_w[te].mean()
for p in (p_logreg, p_knn):
    alpha = np.quantile(p(X[ca]), 1 - 0.5)  # threshold for 50% strong calls
    to_s = p(X[te]) >= alpha
    r = np.where(to_s, ok_s[te], ok_w[te]).mean()
    print(p.__name__, alpha, to_s.mean(), (r - r_w) / (r_s - r_w))

blocks.md:
Results of this run (one random split) on its 1,972 test prompts:

- **Logistic regression**: alpha = 0.4644 from the calibration split; on test it sends 48.7% to the strong model and reaches PGR 0.545. A random router at that share expects PGR 0.487. APGR over ten cost levels: 0.601.
- **kNN vote (k = 50)**: alpha = 0.4600, but the scores are multiples of 1/50, so many prompts tie at the cut and the test share lands at 57.6%; PGR 0.594 against 0.576 for random. APGR 0.630.

In this run both beat random, but not by much at the 50% point, and not reliably: rerun on 11 other random shuffles of the same 9,860 battles, each router fell below random at its calibrated point twice, while APGR stayed between 0.54 and 0.64 every time. That matches RouteLLM's finding that routers trained only on sparse Arena votes are weak, and that adding judge-labeled or golden-labeled data in your domain is what helps most.

blocks.title: Calibration of the logistic-regression router (test split)

scenes.caption: Test prompts sorted by predicted probability into five equal groups. A calibrated router would put each point on the diagonal: among prompts given 0.6, the strong model should win 60% of the time.

Real result: predictions span 0.33 to 0.59, but actual win rates only 0.41 to 0.49. The ranking carries some signal; the numbers themselves are too spread out to read as probabilities, so set alpha from a target share, never from its face value.

blocks.md: **Calibrate alpha on your traffic.** Alpha is a quantile, so it only means "50% strong" for traffic that looks like the calibration set. Split the same data by topic: 941 of the 9,860 prompts mention code (Python, SQL, functions and so on), 190 of them in this run's test split. With alpha calibrated for 50% strong on all calibration prompts, the test set as a whole gets 48.7% strong calls, but the code prompts get 63.2%, although across the whole dataset the strong model's win rate on code prompts (0.476) is barely higher than on the rest (0.462). On this split a coding product would pay for about 13 more points of strong calls than planned; on 11 other shuffles the code prompts got 48% to 68% (57% on average), so the size of the jump is noisy but its direction held 10 times out of 11. Calibrate on a recent sample of your own prompts, for the share you can afford, then measure quality at that point.

blocks.caption: RouteLLM's documented drop-in usage. Not run here: the mf router embeds every prompt with OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small, which needs a paid API key, and the routed calls go to paid model APIs. The model names are the README's 2024 examples; substitute current ones.
blocks.code:
# pip install "routellm[serve,eval]"
from routellm.controller import Controller

client = Controller(
    routers=["mf"],                        # matrix factorization router
    strong_model="gpt-4-1106-preview",
    weak_model="anyscale/mistralai/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1",
)

# Calibrate once (shell): the threshold that sends 50% of Arena prompts to the strong model
#   python -m routellm.calibrate_threshold --routers mf --strong-model-pct 0.5 \
#       --config config.example.yaml
#   For 50.0% strong model calls for mf, threshold = 0.11593

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="router-mf-0.11593",              # router-<name>-<threshold>
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
)

blocks.md: Two details in that output are worth noticing. First, the threshold for a 50% strong share is 0.11593, not 0.5: the mf router's scores are not calibrated probabilities, so only the calibration step tells you what a threshold means. Second, `calibrate_threshold` does nothing clever: it loads precomputed router scores for the prompts of the public Arena dataset and returns the score quantile at 1 minus the target share, exactly what our own script did. The README says so plainly: the share of calls routed to each model will differ based on the queries you actually receive, so calibrate on a sample that resembles your traffic. The OpenAI-compatible server reads the router and threshold from the model name, `router-[ROUTER NAME]-[THRESHOLD]`.

Many teams first put a router in front of their models for **availability** rather than cost: when a provider returns errors, times out or rate-limits you (HTTP 429), send the request somewhere else. In LiteLLM's router, for example:

- `num_retries` retries the same model group first, and `fallbacks` names the model groups to try next once those retries fail.
- `context_window_fallbacks` and `content_policy_fallbacks` catch two specific errors: a prompt too long for the model, and a provider's content refusal.
- `allowed_fails` and `cooldown_time` take a deployment out of rotation for a while after repeated failures.

A fallback is a routing decision with a cost and quality effect like any other: log which model answered. Client-side retries with backoff, Retry-After headers and rate limits are covered in the async-batching-caching course.

blocks.title: Routing for availability: retry, then fall back

scenes.caption: The cost router already chose the primary model for this prompt; the request goes there.
The provider is over its rate limit and answers 429. The router retries within the same model group (with backoff, see the async-batching-caching course), and fails again.
The fallback list names another model group, so the router sends the same request there. That model may be pricier or weaker than the one the cost router chose.
The app gets an answer plus the name of the model that produced it. Log it: fallback traffic is a separate route whose cost and quality you should track.

blocks.md:
**Multi-turn chats.** A router can decide per turn or once per conversation. Per turn looks cheaper on paper but has two hidden costs. Switching models mid-conversation changes tone and formatting, which users notice. And it throws away **provider prompt caching** (the async-batching-caching course explains it): the provider stores its processed state for a prompt's prefix, and on Anthropic a 5-minute cache write costs 1.25x the base input price and a read 0.1x for most models (a few of the newest read for less). That stored state is the model's own internal state, so only the same model can reuse it; each switch makes the next model reprocess, at the write price, every part of the conversation it has not cached yet.

A worked case: a 4,000-token system prompt, then 10 turns of 300 user and 400 answer tokens, at the docs' list prices for Claude Sonnet 4.6 (input USD 3, output 15 per million) as strong and Claude Haiku 4.5 (1 and 5) as weak, every turn cached by its own model.

blocks.title: One 10-turn chat, USD per 1,000 conversations (worked model)

scenes.caption: Routing per conversation with prompt caching: all strong costs 118.92 (58.92 input, 60.00 output), all weak 39.64. Haiku 4.5 caches only prefixes of at least 4,096 tokens; the first turn's 4,300 just clears that.
Routing per turn with turns 1, 4, 7 and 9 on the strong model, you might expect 0.4 x 118.92 + 0.6 x 39.64 = 71.35.

Actual: 95.62. Input alone is 59.62, more than all-strong's 58.92, because each switch makes a model re-read the grown conversation at the write price instead of the read price. Output costs follow the 40/60 mix.

blocks.md:
This is why many systems route per conversation, or keep a conversation on its model and re-route only at natural breaks. LiteLLM's router offers **session affinity** that pins every request of a conversation to the deployment that served its first request, and its docs name provider-side prompt caching as a reason to use it. It works among deployments of one model group; keeping a conversation on one model is still your cost router's job.

Two more production habits:

- **Latency-aware routing** among deployments of the same model: LiteLLM's latency-based strategy tracks response times and picks the fastest deployment.
- **Shadow evaluation and A/B tests.** Send a small sample of weak-routed prompts to the strong model as well, judge both answers offline (with the judge biases of the llm-as-judge course in mind), and track cost and quality per route. That sample is also the fresh, labeled traffic you need to retrain and re-calibrate the router when drift moves the strong-call share.

Every component here changes quietly over time: provider prices, which models are available, the router's score distribution, and your users' prompts. Re-run the calibration on recent traffic on a schedule, alert on the strong-call share and the fallback rate, and keep the shadow sample running.

blocks.question: RouteLLM's calibrate_threshold reports 0.11593 for 50% strong calls. You deploy router-mf-0.11593 for a coding assistant and find 80% of requests going to the strong model. Why?
options: The router is broken and must be retrained from scratch
The threshold was calibrated on Chatbot Arena prompts; your coding prompts get higher scores, so the same threshold sends more of them to the strong model
Thresholds above 0.1 always send most traffic to the strong model
The strong model is rate limiting the weak one
blocks.explain: A threshold is a quantile of the score distribution on the calibration set. Coding prompts look hard to a router trained on Arena data, so their scores sit higher and more of them clear 0.11593. Recompute the quantile on a sample of your own prompts for the share you can afford, then measure quality there.

blocks.question: A chat product routes every turn independently and sends 40% of turns to the strong model. Its input-token bill is about the same as sending every turn to the strong model. What is the most likely cause?
options: The router's scores are miscalibrated
Output tokens are counted as input tokens
Switching models between turns discards each model's cached conversation prefix, so every switch re-processes the whole history at full (cache write) price
The weak model is more expensive per token
blocks.explain: Prompt caching is per model. With caching, staying on one model pays about 0.1x for the long history on each turn; a switch pays 1.25x for all the history the other model has not cached yet. Route per conversation, or pin conversations to a model (session affinity) and re-route only when the context is short.
